explanation: It grows in boggy coastal plains where regular wildfires stop taller plants shading it out. Its trap shuts when trigger hairs are touched more than once in quick succession, so raindrops rarely fool it.

claims.text: The Venus flytrap grows wild in wetlands of North and South Carolina in the United States.
The Venus flytrap does not grow wild in the Amazon rainforest, on Borneo or in Madagascar.
Venus flytrap habitat depends on regular fires that keep taller plants from shading the flytraps.
A Venus flytrap's trap closes when its trigger hairs are touched more than once within a short time.
Needing repeated touches helps the trap avoid closing on raindrops and debris.

results.title: How does the Venus flytrap work?
Species Status Assessment For Venus Flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) Version 1.1

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula): It grows wild only on the East Coast of the U.S., in the Carolinas. Outside cultivation, it is native only to the coastal bogs of North and South Carolina, specifically within a 100-kilometer (62-mile) radius of Wilmington, North Carolina. Its habitat is nutrient-poor wetlands. It is found in bogs, wet savannahs, and canebrakes. Populations outside that area in Florida and Washington state are naturalized or introduced, not native.

claimResults.note: Kew (Plants of the World Online), the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Britannica and Wikipedia are in the list. The naturalized Florida and Washington populations are not among the options, so no second answer. The sunflower half of this query returned nothing; p.nat.0150 has its own search.

evidence.restatement: Dionaea is endemic to the coastal plain of the Carolinas and does not grow wild in the Amazon, on Borneo or in Madagascar.
Its wet pine savannas need frequent fires to clear taller competitors; fire suppression is one of its main threats.
The trap shuts when trigger hairs are touched twice within roughly 20 to 30 seconds.
The two-touch rule keeps single touches such as raindrops or debris from springing the trap.
The Venus flytrap is native only to a small coastal area of North and South Carolina.

claimResults.note: High-risk (checker_doubt): this record rests on knowledge, so the claim needs external evidence in check A (section 9.9).

evidence.restatement: It does not grow wild in the Amazon, on Borneo or in Madagascar; the pitcher plants there are different plants.
Its bog and savanna habitat depends on regular fire that keeps taller plants from shading it.
The trap closes when a trigger hair is touched twice within about twenty seconds.
The two-touch rule stops the trap closing on raindrops and debris.

editor.reason: A and B pass; all 5 claims confirmed in both checks; high-risk c1 (web in A). Style, distractors and balance reviewed. The key's form ('The Carolinas, USA') differs from the three tropical options, but the tropical guess is the trap and the estimate is 0.30.
